drance that may exist, I am convinced that I would have helped effectively to improve the social climate, the economic conditions and the political issues in this country. I am in favour, for my part, of a new constitution, a constitution in which not only the responsibilities and rights of the various levels of government will be clearly defined, their sources of revenues to meet their obligations, so that we will stop wasting so much time in useless conferences that do not solve anything.
So, Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate on Bill C-56,1 wanted to put forward very positive ideas and, hopefully, work with all my colleagues in this House to create a greater harmony in this country, so that Canadians in eastern, central and western Canada can be proud of having equal opportunities all across this country and we are no longer led to believe that a part of the country is giving handouts to the other out of sheer kindness. Are we living in the same country or not? If we are living in the same country, our responsibility at the national level is to provide good administration for everyone and not have part of the people believe that one part of the country is doing the other favours out of generosity.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps my words will be judged as coming from a man who has not much confidence at this point precisely because of the situation created by that issue we are now discussing and because of the $186 million, but $186 million is not much compared with the whole future of a people and a country. Let us disregard that $186 million barrier and build a real constitution, so that we may have a real prosperous country in which all Canadians today and tomorrow will be proud to live.

Mr. Speaker, in the six years in which I have been in the House I have risen to speak on many occasions, but never have I felt as much desire to speak out as I do today. I have never felt so strongly about an issue. I have never listened so attentively to all the arguments which have been presented by members of the opposition, and by others outside this House, on the subject of this bill, Bill C-56. I have never on any issue been as convinced as I am today of the wisdom of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in his objective, in his method, and in the presentation of the bill before us. With all my English logic I have listened to the arguments presented. I can say, frankly and honestly, that I do not understand them. I have looked at the emotional side. Perhaps I am not very emotional, but I have tried to look at the subject from an emotional point of view to see whether I could better understand the extraordinary attitude and point of view which have been put forward in opposition to the bill.
I find it extraordinary we should be discussing today what Canada is all about. We are seeking to determine, in this argument on the provincial sales tax measure, what kind of Canada we want for the future. I hope we will never write a constitution which would make it impossible to carry on a

dialogue between the provincial and federal levels of government.
When the minister presented this bill to the House he clearly outlined his objective in making the proposals he did. Economists throughout the country had almost unanimously agreed that the best way to stimulate the economy was to reduce provincial sales taxes across the land to provide immediate stimulus to purchasing which would, hopefully, result in increased investment, increased manufacturing, and greater employment opportunities.
The minister was faced with the obvious problem that provincial sales tax is under provincial jurisdiction. He has acknowledged this right from the start. The method he proposed-and really the only method available to him-was to use federal taxes as a compensation if the provincial governments were willing to accept the scheme he proposed.
After three weeks of argument the minister obtained the agreement of nine of the ten finance ministers. A couple of them decided to make alternative proposals in forms which were acceptable to the federal minister. During those three weeks the Quebec minister of finance never said a word. He did not say, "Mr. Chretien, this is provincial jurisdiction; stay out; do not touch". He kept his mouth shut because he was playing games. One could consider our Minister of Finance perhaps a little naive because he thought intelligence might override these emotional game considerations.
The timing is what I find difficult to understand. The federal budget was brought down on April 10. The Quebec provincial budget was brought down on April 18. We have talked a lot about what was understood regarding how moneys were going to be raised and how the transfer was going to be made.
In the budget of Mr. Parizeau of April 18, at the bottom of page 22 he acknowledges-and it is printed-that the method of transfer would be by a reduction in federal taxes paid by the taxpayers. I do not know how long it takes to print a document such as the document I have in my hand, but I would suggest that such a document was put together even before the federal budget of April 10. Iam not inclined to believe that there was any misunderstanding whatsoever in the mind of the Quebec Minister of Finance prior to the presentation of the federal budget on April 10.
On April 12 the Quebec Minister of Finance made a counter proposal. On April 21 the federal Minister of Finance suggested a different form for his original proposal. This, incidentally, should certainly answer one of the points raised by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) when he spoke of the differences between Quebec and the maritime provinces. The counter proposal of the federal Minister of Finance was to provide an opportunity for Quebec to be treated in the same way as the maritimes. The federal minister was prepared, if Quebec was willing, to cut 2 per cent from the sales tax on the remainder of products to which sales tax was still applicable.
May 18, 1978

He was prepared to go along with the same proposition he made to the ministers of finance of the maritime provinces.
The minister of finance of the province of Quebec, Mr. Parizeau, insisted that the full value of the budget offer be provided toward the cost of the selective cut which he had chosen to make in Quebec. I suggest that, as it stands right now, that is exactly what is being done. By vacating an amount of $85 per taxpayer in the federal field the federal minister makes it possible for Quebec to occupy the field in the same amount-or a varying amount, if it so wishes-so that it can be compensated fully for the provincial sales tax cuts instituted. No one in the province of Quebec would suffer.
There is one point upon which I want to dwell. Many speakers have spoken about the so-called unfairness of the deduction of federal tax from the incomes of those who pay taxes. It has been said that this is not fair to the poor who do not pay taxes, or to old people. With all the logic I could muster I have tried to understand this point, but one thing I do understand is that a sales tax cut is applicable to all those who make purchases. Poor people make smaller purchases than rich people do, so by its very nature a sales tax cut aids those who have money much more than it aids those who do not. What this has to do with the transfer of tax field from the federal level to the provincial level I do not understand.
We are saying that in eight of the provinces where the scheme is applicable we are taking $100 out of one pocket and putting $100 into the other pocket. In those eight provinces where the federal government collects provincial taxes, the individual who pays taxes is not even aware that there has been a transaction.
The province of Quebec is the only province which has decided to collect its own provincial taxes. That is its right, but that costs the people of Quebec many millions of dollars. I am told the cost is $120 million. That is what the people of Quebec are paying so that the Quebec provincial government can exercise its right. However, because the Quebec government chooses to exercise that right, there is no simple solution for Quebec by which the federal government can, as it is doing in the other eight provinces, take $100 out of one pocket and put $100 into another pocket. The money must first be given to the taxpayer. In the case of Quebec the amount is $85 for the simple reason that the federal government has already agreed to reimburse two percentage points of the eight percentage points that have been eliminated from the sales tax on shoes, furniture, and clothing.
So we give the taxpayer $85, and we say to the Quebec minister of finance, "You have chosen to tax your people yourself. Now you can make a choice. You can choose to tax them the same $85". The Quebec government can choose to tax the people of Quebec on some sliding scale in order to bring in the same amount, or it can choose not to tax them, if it wishes. However, it is the Quebec government's field, and it is Quebec's decision.
There has been so much misunderstanding that I want to refer briefly-as did the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Income Tax Act
Lambert)-to an editorial which appeared in Le Devoir on Tuesday of last week.
It has been called the confrontation between the two ministers of finance, and I suppose that one cannot deny that it is an emotional confrontation. I do not know why we should be surprised.
In one case we have the federal Minister of Finance who believes in a Canada with ten provinces joined together willingly, and in the other case we have the Quebec minister of finance whose avowed intention is to destroy the country as we know it today, and whose avowed intention is to separate. So it should be no surprise to anyone that, no matter what the Canadian Minister of Finance proposes, it is going to be rejected by the Quebec minister of finance. He has no reason for reaching an agreement, and I might suggest that if anybody has sat for weeks and weeks on end across the table at a bargaining session between employer and union one would know right away whether one is going to reach an agreement or whether one is entering into an exercise in futility where the intention is not to reach an agreement.
I suggest that under the present circumstances the objective of the Quebec minister of finance is not to reach an agreement, and there is no way in which he is going to reach an agreement because, if he did, he would be illustrating that federalism works, which he has no intention of doing.
Hear, hear!

The article in Le Devoir to which I referred mentions the intervention of the Canadian Minister of Finance in a provincial jurisdiction. That is admitted. I suggest that the day that a federal minister of finance is not able to sit down with his provincial counterparts to try to reach an agreement, we might as well call it quits, give up on Canada, and start carving it up right away. He did just that, and I suggest that three weeks is a long enough time for anyone to say, "I do not like what you are doing. I am not going to accept what you are doing. Go away and don't talk to me."
It should be remembered-and I think the point has to be raised-that this federal Liberal government was dealing with ten provinces of which only two have Liberal governments. So the federal Minister of Finance had to deal with Conservative, right-wing ministers of finance, and also with socialist, leftwing ministers of finance. But these gentlemen-and I call them gentlemen advisedly-were willing to sit down, and whilst they might not have been very happy, whilst they might not have liked the deal that was being suggested, they were willing to discuss it and come to an agreement. I suggest that despite the proposal afterwards of four ministers from the west, even those four provinces, Alberta included, were willing to come to an agreement.
To suggest that the Canadian Minister of Finance, after having presented his budget and after seeing the action of the Quebec minister of finance, should play into the Parizeau track and hand over to the Quebec government the balance of

the funds allocated for specific purposes, seems to me to ignore the fact completely that there are ten provinces in Canada and that an agreement was already reached with nine.
In the new constitution, which we will obviously be discussing soon, we should consider very carefully to what degree we want to allow the power of veto to prevent any further agreement or any further change. As I have mentioned before, the extreme is if that provincial power of veto is to extend to the province of Prince Edward Island, and I am not at the moment criticizing that province for any other reason than to say that it is a province that has a population smaller than the constituency which I represent. I think we have to think very carefully about our attitude toward a constitution that will completely stymie any future progress. I suggest that if we believe that we must at all times have the full agreement of the ten provinces, then we are in effect saying that at no time are we going to be able to have any future agreements between the provincial and federal governments.
Even the point about the distribution of the funds to the Quebec federal taxpayer being inequitable I find difficult to swallow, for the simple reason that the 2.4 million taxpayers in the province of Quebec cover almost all the families in Quebec. I suggest also that the $85 which will go to every taxpayer is far more beneficial to those who are only paying $100 or $200 in federal sales taxes than would be the total of either the 8 per cent on furniture, shoes and clothing, or the 2 per cent across the board on the total purchases at that period of time.
What I am suggesting is that $85 for every taxpayer is a fairer distribution than either the 8 per cent formula or the 2 per cent formula initially proposed by the Minister of Finance. Again I find it difficult to follow the logic of the argument that even if this $85 per taxpayer is of benefit-and it is not intended to be a benefit-that it is inequitable.
I have one las. point to make, and I see it is nearly five o'clock, Mr. Speaks:.
If the minister of finance of the province of Quebec is not prepared to deal his hand while Quebec is still part of Canada, then how is he going to deal with Canada under sovereignty association?

He said: Mr. Speaker, in entering the debate on the motions, to which you have just referred, I would point out that the debate arises from the government's refusal to release documents bearing on the uranium cartel. These are remarkable documents, Mr. Speaker, the most remarkable documents I have seen in my five years in this House, because they paint an incredible picture of administration officials conspiring with uranium producers to fix prices, set quotas, and rig bids in an effort to raise the price of uranium.
Even worse, these documents tell a chilling story of how government officials coached worried uranium producers in ways of circumventing the laws of the land, in ways of "minimizing the risks under the Combines Investigation Act." These are serious matters in themselves, so serious that they would warrant the release of the documents to a concerned House.
There is another more important point; one salient fact about these documents that I ask hon. members to bear in mind during this debate; and that is that a great many of these documents are now readily available in the United States. They are available to the United States Congress, to American courts in at least three states, to two federal and state investigative bodies and, in fact, they are available to any American who wants them and requests them of his government. All in all, something like 90 per cent of the documents I have requested from this government are available right now in the United States. Yet this administration has consistently denied them to this House.
The government went even further in suppressing this information. For the first time in Canadian history, the government moved retroactively to deny these documents, or any other information about the cartel, to Canadians. It passed an order in council to make it a crime for Canadians even to discuss the cartel. That order in council has been modified somewhat, but it still applies to members of government and industry who were involved in the cartel. In other words, anyone who knows anything about the cartel is still forbidden to shed any light on the matter. Such a move by a Canadian government is an insult to us all. To state my case as simply as possible, it is ludicrous that we in this House, and the Canadian people in general, should have to turn to United States tribunals for information about the activities of our own government, information which should rightly come from Ottawa.
We will undoubtedly hear many excuses from the government tonight why this House cannot be trusted with these documents. We will be told again-just as we have been told consistently over the past eight months-that the release of these documents is detrimental to our foreign relations, and in some strange manner would assist the extra-territorial application of United States law.
The central point I urge hon. members to consider as they listen to these arguments is that most of these documents are already in the hands of those foreign tribunals. They are there now. They were there when we asked for them last August. The only thing this administration accomplishes by denying them to Canadians is to humiliate this House and the Canadi-
Uranium Cartel
an people by making us look abroad for the information which should be forthcoming right here at home.
It is a sad mistake this government is making, and I for one think it is tragic that Canadians should once again be the last to find out what their government has been up to.
The second point we hope this House will consider is that this government has attracted widespread attention around the world for its efforts in setting up this cartel. It is incumbent upon this House to ensure that Canadians too-not just Americans, but Canadians as well-are given an opportunity to scrutinize first-hand the activities which have generated so much interest elsewhere. In other words, it is incumbent upon this House to ensure Canadians access to information about the uranium cartel at a time when that cartel is the object of such controversy abroad.
This is clearly no ordinary request for routine or ordinary documents. The "harmless", "informal marketing arrangement", to use their words, described by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), has been stripped of its respectability by recent investigations and has been revealed to be the world's first international energy cartel since the end of the second world war. It showed OPEC how to do it. It is probably one of the most successful as well.
The price of uranium has shot up 700 per cent since Ottawa began its little adventure in marketing in 1972, and concerned electricity consumers and utilities around the world are combing through these documents for an understanding of how all this came about.
In the United States the cartel has become the subject of a congressional investigation in Washington, and an investigation by the New York state assembly. Ottawa's marketing agreement has found its way into lawsuits in Illinois, Virginia, New Mexico, and Pennsylvania, where the cartel has become the cornerstone in the largest and most complex round of civil litigations in U.S. history with claims and counterclaims in excess of $10 billion. In one of these lawsuits, a utility, the Tennessee Valley Authority, has named several Canadian uranium producers in a multimillion dollar action.
More recently the cartel was the subject of an 18-month United States federal grand jury that ended in a so-called "informational" indictment against Gulf Oil Corporation, and could possibly result in a number of civil actions against other cartel participants.
In short, this government has made history, though of a somewhat dubious sort. It has set up the first energy cartel and, in the process, has become embroiled in history's largest round of lawsuits. The judiciaries of three states and no less than two arms of the U.S. federal government are currently rummaging through the dirty linen surrounding this fiasco, and this administration still feels that the parliament and people of Canada cannot be trusted with a first hand look at what all the fuss is about. "Trust me", the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says. That is the sum total of everything he has told this House about the cartel, "Trust me and I'll tell you everything you need to know. And right now the only thing

you need to know is that the cartel is basically harmless. It didn't cause uranium prices to rise; the Arabs did. And anyway, it was the only way government could help a struggling industry."
We know from these documents that this simply is not so, Mr. Speaker. Three of the documents we requested detail very specifically how the cartel secretly conspired to take the price of uranium from $6 a pound in 1972 to over $18 a pound by the end of 1974. A 300 per cent increase in any commodity is not negligible, it is very substantial regardless of what this government says. As a result, the cartel we are discussing will have repercussions for the consumers of electricity as long as uranium is used to fuel nuclear generators.
If hon. members think my remarks are partisan in nature, then I refer them to a preliminary report on the cartel prepared by the Hon. Irwin J. Landes, chairman of the New York Committee on Corporations, Authorities and Commissions. Mr. Landes says very simply:
From the information already developed by our staff, we are now beginning to re-evaluate New York's plans for nuclear energy development.
One of the reasons the state was seriously considering nuclear options was the assumed low cost of nuclear fuel.
We believe the cartel has set in motion price increases which put in doubt whether nuclear energy will continue to be a low cost energy source.
The unique process of rate-setting allows the increased costs to flow directly through to the taxpayers.
In New York state, it is our belief that price increases set in motion by the cartel could cost consumers $1 billion in New York alone between now and 1980.
Here in Canada where ambitious plans are under way for nuclear development in Ontario, New Brunswick, and possibly Quebec, the cost to consumers could be equally as high.
In New Mexico, Judge Edwin Felter was also unimpressed with arguments that the cartel has had little effect on energy costs. In a judgment that could cost a subsidiary of a cartel participant $1.2 billion, Judge Felter ruled as follows:
The purpose and effect of the cartel was to limit the supply, control the production, allocate markets and fix the price of uranium.
He added:
The cartel agreements were carried out effectively-the world market price of uranium was fixed at artificially high levels by the cartel.
He said that, contrary to the government's claims, the cartel pursued a "policy of secrecy... that expressly included" domestic markets.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that while I have no personal interest one way or another in the outcome of the American litigation, I think it is important for this House to remember that two different independent inquiries in the United States have taken radically different views of the cartel than that put forward by this Trudeau emperor administration. I can think of no reason why either the Moss committee, the grand jury, or Judge Felter would take a partisan interest in Canadian politics, and we must ask ourselves why-in all the serious inquiry to date about the cartel-this administration alone views the cartel as basically innocent?

At any event, whether the Americans are looking for scapegoats for high energy costs that they themselves may be responsible for, or whether this administration is simply whitewashing the whole sorry mess, I think it is important that Canadians be given an opportunity to judge this matter for themselves. It is important that Canadians be given a clear and unimpeded view of the cartel, and these documents which, I repeat, are already in most cases available in the United States, are necessary for such an understanding.
I want to turn to one final matter before summing up. We have heard before, and we will no doubt hear again tonight, attempts to equate this reasonable request for documents with some ridiculous allegations that we on this side of the House are insensitive to the needs of the Canadian uranium industry, or that we are somehow "on the side of the Americans" to the detriment of Canadian interests. Nothing could be further from the truth, and I want to set the record straight.
There is no doubt that the uranium industry in the late sixties and early seventies was in trouble. The cutbacks in the British and American arms programs, as well as protective measures taken in the United States, had the effect of depressing uranium prices. Initiating a cartel was not the only way to help our industry. The cartel records show over and over again that other options were open to government if it wanted to assist a troubled industry. At least three of the documents I have requested spell out very clearly that this government could have set up a uranium marketing board, as it has with wheat, for example. It could put legislation before this House to ensure a two-price system that would raise world prices for uranium producers while protecting domestic users against excessive prices. In other words, Mr. Speaker, there were perfectly legal and open ways of coming to the rescue of a Canadian industry, ways in which Canadians, producers and consumers alike, could be protected. What disturbs us is not that the government moved to help our uranium producers, but that it chose secret, backroom conspiracies, with little regard for the Canadian consumer or the laws of the country.
There are today many thousands of Canadian jobs in the steel, footware, textile, nickel, copper, agricultural, and furniture industries that are just as endangered as those in the uranium industry in 1972. Yet no one would suggest that that gives government, or the industries carte blanche to violate the laws of the land, especially if perfectly legal and acceptable means exist to help those industries.
The government is trying to paint this whole episode with the broad brush of respectability, but I suggest that if nothing is wrong with the government's actions in the cartel then it has nothing to fear from releasing these documents to the Canadian people.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, it is vital to the democratic process of review of government that these documents be released. Even if all of them were heretofore undisclosed, it would be in the best interests of an open and candid government to allow public scrutiny. The insanity of the situation is that documents requested in 23 out of 36 of my motions were already released by the Moss committee when we requested them from this

I hope the government uses this debate tonight to end this ridiculous charade and release to Canadians what others have free access to already. We hope it will permit the Canadian people to make a candid and frank assessment of the cartel that was built secretly in the boardrooms of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. After all, the Canadian public will be paying for it for a long time to come.
I am pleased that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is in the House this evening. I hope he will respond to my request in a positive way. There is, frankly, absolutely nothing in any document to which I have referred, or to which I refer in the motions, that should not be disclosed to the Canadian public. It is a sordid tale, Mr. Speaker, a tale of a government more concerned with cover-up and hiding facts than of levelling with the Canadian people. Perhaps the worst example of a government conspiracy to break the laws of Canada has been this instance of the uranium cartel fiasco.
In another jurisdiction we know what happened to the senior executive when they chose to break the laws of that land. In this country, unfortunately, we have a different system. In this country we would not have had a Watergate investigation, because basically if Mr. Nixon had been the Prime Minister of this country his consent would have had to be sought for the investigation. If Mr. Nixon were then to act in the way our emperor, the Prime Minister, acts in respect of the uranium cartel, the investigation would never have taken place.

The hon. member sketched out a great deal of the history of the uranium mining industry when he was speaking, and I would hope he would allow the same degree of latitude on this side of the House. It seems to me that not only the hon. member for York-Simcoe but many of the members in this House have been greatly concerned with the uranium mining industry and the difficulties it experienced in the 1970s and 1960s which have led to the more favourable situation existing today.
I would like to remind the hon. member that this industry was not always as fortunate as it is today. The exact documents that he is talking about have some relationship to that difficulty-
Let's see them.

I was mentioning that by 1955 negotiations had been completed for the sale of uranium concentrates to the extent of $300 million for the deposits located in the various parts of Canada.
The town of Elliot Lake was created to house the people needed to extract the uranium produced from the vast low-grade ores in that area. By 1959 shipments from Ontario, mostly from Elliot Lake, had reached an annual rate of 12,746 tons of uranium concentrates valued at some $269 million. Production from Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories brought Canadian production in that year to almost 16,000 tons with a value of some $331 million; the highest for any mineral or metal exported from Canada in that year.
Of more importance is the employment which this uranium industry provided. In 1959 Canada had 19 uranium mills and 23 mines providing direct employment for some 13,600 people. The boom in uranium production was spurred by special price incentives offered by the United States, through Eldorado Mining and Refining, to obtain uranium for its military programs.
In November, 1959, the United States Atomic Energy Commission announced it would not take up its options to purchase additional uranium, so the industry had to substantially readjust downwards its scale of operations. As early as January, 1960, the number employed by the uranium mining industry in Canada had dropped by almost 2,000 to some 11,800, of which 8,500 were employed in the Elliot Lake area alone. Throughout 1960 the layoffs accelerated, so that by the end of 1960 employment in the uranium industry in Canada had declined to 6,000, of which 4,000 were in the Elliot Lake area.
Mines continued to close, so that the Canadian government in 1963 instituted the first of a series of stockpile programs to maintain the semblance of a uranium industry. Even with these programs, only three mining operations continued operating in Canada between 1964 and 1975, Eldorado Nuclear Limited in the Beaverlodge area of northern Saskatchewan, and Rio Algom and Denison Mines in the Elliot Lake region of Ontario. By 1971 employment in the uranium industry in Canada had declined to less than 2,300 employees, about 17 per cent of the peak employment in 1959. This employment was only maintained by the stockpiling programs of the

Canadian government and those instituted by the producers themselves.
The community of Elliot Lake declined with the misfortunes of the Canadian uranium mining industry. The population in 1960, just at the start of the market crash, was some 25,000. By 1966 the population had declined to less than 6,700. Some recovery took place with the negotiation of contracts in the late 1960s with the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority and with Japanese utilities. A gradual return to the mining community took place so that by 1969 its population was some 9,500.
Growing concern with the limited market potential and the accumulating producer stockpiles threatened the well-being of the community again. And thus, in 1970 the government had to institute another stockpiling program. This one was a joint venture with Denison Mines to maintain a production level of 2,000 tons of yellow cake per year over the period 1971 to 1974.
Historically, about 70 per cent to 75 per cent of the world's uranium production has been in Canada and the United States, with the United States taking the major share of the production after the market collapse of the 1960s and the institution of the United States Atomic Energy Commission's restrictions on the enrichment of uranium for use in nuclear reactors within the United States.
In 1958 and 1959 for example, Canada's share of world uranium production was 37 per cent and the United States share 35 per cent to 38 per cent. By 1968 Canada's share dropped to 16 per cent while the United States share increased to 54 per cent. Canada's share would have been even less without the stockpiling policies of the Canadian government and private producers.
Not only Canadian producers were facing the dilemma of production over-capacity and the accumulation of stockpiles. Other non-U.S. uranium producers were also facing the same problems. In 1971 and 1972 the international uranium market was in a chaotic condition because of over-capacity, the accumulating stockpiles in both private industry and government warehouses, and because of the continuing efforts of some consuming utilities to play off one producer against another so as to reduce the price paid for uranium to an absolute minimum. Market deterioration was so serious in fact that some uranium sales were made at below $4 per pound of yellow cake, less than the operating costs alone for many producers in the world. Uranium policies originating in the United States served to exacerbate the difficulties being encountered by the producing industry.
Faced with the chaotic marketing conditions, the government had several options. The first of these was to let the uranium industry collapse. I assume that is what the hon. member for York-Simcoe probably would have done. The second choice was to continue with yet another expensive stockpiling program; the first three cost the Canadian taxpayer some $129 million. The third option was to try to alleviate the problem through discussions with government representatives
May 18, 1978

of consuming nations; and fourth was to explore an arrangement with government officials of producing countries.
Following the first option would have been irresponsible and would have negated the efforts which had been followed in the 1960s to protect the industry. To follow the second option, that of stockpiling, would have only exacerbated the problem by creating more stockpiles to over-hang the market and deter its eventual recovery.
While the Canadian government had no success by its interventions in the 1960s to have the United States government reconsider its policies which were damaging the Canadian uranium industry, the then minister of energy, mines and resources and his officials did discuss the problem in 1971 with government representatives of consuming nations. One of the dangers envisaged was that, in the face of both devastating competition and unprofitable operations for producers, little or no exploration was likely to be undertaken in order to prove up the enormous quantities of uranium that would be required for the 1980s and beyond. The reactions to the Canadian concern were negative or neutral.
Lacking any positive results from these discussions, the Canadian government authorized officials of two Crown corporations, Eldorado Nuclear, Limited and Uranium Canada, Limited to meet with international uranium producers to discuss possible marketing arrangements for the non-U.S. market. The government also requested private producers to attend. The discussions led to an informal marketing arrangement which excluded the domestic markets of France, South Africa, Australia and Canada, and the United States domestic market.
The Canadian government was informed of and approved the marketing arrangements negotiated by Canadian uranium producers and supported the arrangements in Canada by issuing a regulation under section 9 of the Atomic Energy Control Act controlling such aspects as the minimum selling prices and volumes of sales to export markets. In essence, the government had decided that uranium should not be sold below what was considered to be a reasonable price for this non-renewable resource, and the amount to be exported should be distributed on an equitable basis among the several producing companies in Canada. While the minimum prices acceptable to Canada were revised on several occasions as prices recovered from their distressed levels, they were almost without exception below those reported for the protected United States market, and the last minimum price schedule sent to the Atomic Energy Control Board by the then minister of energy, mines and resources, Mr. Macdonald, on March 6, 1974 were far below the prices which prevail today.
The uranium price spiral of 1975 and 1976 was not caused by the uranium marketing arrangement but by factors outside the control of either the Canadian government or those producers who participated in the arrangement. Shortly after the Arab oil embargo was imposed and the price of imported oil increased four-fold, several countries declared an intention to
Uranium Cartel
expand markedly their nuclear power programs. Soon there developed an attitude among many utilities around the world that longer term purchasing arrangements for uranium should be negotiated and that, if necessary, a stockpiling policy should be adopted.
Then the United States Atomic Energy Commission proposed to relax the embargo on utilization of foreign uranium enriched in the U.S. facilities, and it soon became apparent that there was not enough uranium to supply all those requests that suddenly appeared in the market.
Canadian producers in early 1974 quoted prices of $12.50 per pound U308, well above the then current Canadian government's minimum directed price. At about the same time, curtailment of marketing activities occurred for diverse reasons in Australia, France, South Africa and other African countries. The curtailments placed even more strain on Canadian producers to meet the rising demand. Within the next few months, future Canadian sales of 45,000 tons U3Og had been negotiated, ten times the current annual production in total. By the end of 1974, the world market price had reached about $15 per pound, essentially double that prevailing a year earlier.
The upward price spiral continued during 1975 for a variety of reasons. One reason was related to the fact that the light water reactor industry around the world, dependent as it was on U.S. enrichment, had decided from various USAEC announcements that the tails assay would probably be increased from 0.2 per cent to 0.25 per cent by 1977 and then to 0.3 per cent by 1981. Such a change would represent an increase in uranium feed requirements to the enrichment plant of some 20 per cent. Furthermore, there was a growing conviction that uranium and plutonium recycling from spent fuel was becoming less likely because of regulatory delays and actions by interveners in the United States.
Then came the announcement by U.S. Westinghouse in September 1975 that it would be unable to deliver some 32,500 tons U3Og which it had contracted to sell to various utilities in the United States and abroad. The effects of this action contributed substantially to an increasing rise in the price of uranium as utilities sought to cover their shortfall by rushing into the market. As a consequence, the price reached the $40 level in early 1976.
For the past two years the market price has remained more or less stable with some slight upward adjustment to take account of inflation. This is despite the very marked slowdown in the rate of ordering and delays in construction of nuclear capacity. Requirements for uranium have not responded to this slower growth rate because many utilities made commitments to provide uranium deliveries to the U.S. enrichment plants based on nuclear programs envisaged in the early 1970s. So far the U.S. has not relieved their customers of these obligations.
Actions taken by the Canadian government in supporting the uranium marketing arrangement have assured a sound future for Canada's uranium industry. Production in 1977 from all Canadian uranium producers was some 7,500 tons U3Og compared to the 4,100 ton level in 1971, just prior to the

events which led to the marketing arrangement. Production is expected to increase to some 16,000 tons U3Og by 1985, of which some 7,500 tons will be in the Elliot Lake area. In response to this increase in industrial activity, Elliot Lake is expected to grow from 12,000 today to 42,000 by 1985 or 1986.
Even though the marketing arrangement was not instrumental in the price increases which have taken place since 1974, Canada has benefited from the incentive it provided to companies to expand their exploration efforts. In the early 1970s when prices were abnormally low, there was essentially no incentive for uranium exploration in Canada and the level of expenditure in uranium exploration was less than $4 million per year. From 1974, exploration activity responded to the rapid rise in uranium price so that today the rate of expenditure on uranium exploration is in the order of $70 million per year. Promising new discoveries were made in 1975, 1976 and 1977 at Key Lake, Collins Bay, Midwest River and Maurice Bay in northern Saskatchewan. This can only lead to increased assurances of uranium supplies for both the domestic and export markets and the continued expansion of a sound uranium industry in Canada.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe has not been able to find many takers for his argument that the price of uranium has been pushed up by the marketing arrangement which Canada entered into with other countries of the world. For example, I have with me a letter from the chairman of the board of Denison Mines Limited, Mr. Stephen Roman, who was a political associate and was a supporter politically of the hon. member for York-Simcoe. Another Otto Lang.

The allegations made by Mr. Stevens and his friends are completely unfounded and are, in fact, an irresponsible attempt to discredit the Canadian government and the Canadian uranium industry. Not only are the allegations unjust and baseless, they impugn the integrity of our company, our employees and, by association, our shareholders.
That is the view of the chairman of Denison Mines. There are several other interesting items further on. This is a letter sent not to the government but to the shareholders, and in it he refutes-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

Call it a formal agreement, if you like, but we are still dealing with an informal arrangement. Let us not quibble about words. Canada was a party to an arrangement with other countries; that is my point.
The hon. member for Hastings suggested it would embarrass the government if copies of the documents were made public. When you enter into an agreement with other countries regarding the marketing of uranium and accept certain obliga-

tions as a member of that club-and the Canadian government did that-it should be important to put on the record that other countries which were also part of the arrangement took action in their countries to ensure that the documentation associated with that so-called cartel arrangement would not be made public.
The Australian parliament passed legislation which is, I am told, in every respect just as stringent as the order in council which was passed by this government. The British government, through its attorney general, has taken the case to the House of Lords. I am sure hon. members are aware of that. The French government has taken action. Other governments which were party to this arrangement have taken action to protect their interests - yes, their sovereignty too - because their industries were also faced with survival situations.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe has not said anything about that. He suggested that Canada could forget the fact that it entered into an arrangement with other sovereign countries to protect, in a collective sense, the interests of an important industry in those sovereign countries. speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
That was the reason we took that action. The effect of that regulation was to provide an exemption from the Combines Investigation Act since the board was effectively regulating the volume of exports pursuant to an act of parliament.
The board I am referring to here is the Atomic Energy Control Board. The jurisprudence under that act holds that, in so far as the activities of an industry are effectively regulated, they cannot be in violation of the Combines Investigation Act. The regulation did not operate so as to exempt the producers from any activity which might unduly lessen competition in the domestic market, as it was the government's policy that the domestic market be excluded from the marketing arrangements. While we have no reason to believe that the arrangement did violate the Combines Investigation Act, it was because of the need to resolve allegations that it had done so that my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, directed the director of investigation and research to conduct a formal inquiry under the Combines Investigation Act. That inquiry is now well under way and has had full access to documents and other material in respect of the marketing arrangement.
We do not believe there was any contravention of the Combines Investigation Act because the so-called cartel excluded the Canadian market, as it excluded the U.S. market and the markets of each of the member countries I have mentioned. However, just in case there was, and to meet allegations, action was taken to ensure that the Canadian public interest would be protected, and the director of combines investigations has had, as I have indicated, full access to the documents and will in due course be making his report.

Why not a marketing board?

game when we negotiate together in a reasonable spirit, being desirous of having some kind of an agreement.

provincial tax because we live in the province of Quebec than we would pay in the province of Ontario.

He says that in the province of Quebec more goods are produced by other countries and provinces, and he quotes, for example, the shoe industry, in respect of which only 22 per cent of shoes sold in Quebec are made in the province of Quebec; more than 22 per cent are made in Ontario and 54 per cent are imported.
