The same thing applies in respect of furniture, with only 30 per cent of the furniture sold in Quebec being made in Quebec. In respect of textiles, 24 per cent are made in Quebec. Once again, if there is an inequity or stupidity it is in the inference that the 8 per cent tax reduction is good just for Quebec. The 8 per cent reduction in tax in Quebec is as much of assistance to provinces such as Ontario as it is to Quebec, and the Quebec people should realize that. In the meantime, because there is not a 2 per cent reduction on other products, other industries of manufacture in Quebec are not getting any benefit.
We have often talked about the fact that Quebec purchases goods from Ontario and Ontario purchases goods from Quebec. The difference is that 20 per cent of Quebec purchases are made in Ontario and only about half as many, 11 per cent, of Ontario purchases are made in Quebec. The obvious inference is that Quebec is much more dependent on Ontario than Ontario is on Quebec.
One last point I would like to make concerning figures is that whereas today the federal tax is approximately 40 per cent of the total tax take of the three levels of government- federal, provincial and municipal-some years ago the situation was reversed. Quite obviously there is less power in the hands of the federal government today to adjust various factors, to adjust the economy, as a result of this smaller portion of the taxing power that the federal government has. In addition, despite the fact the federal portion has dropped from approximately 60 per cent to today's 40 per cent, included in the federal portion today are all the programs of redistribution of incomes which are surely a direct benefit to the

provinces and particularly to the have-not provinces such as the province of Quebec.
As far as the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) is concerned-and I feel that everybody has been very hypocritical in their remarks on this particular bill-he talks about interference in provincial jurisdiction and yet only today he proposes a motion criticizing the government of Russia. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we have a right to attempt to interfere in the jurisdictions of other countries-and bearing in mind that the same motion that was proposed today was proposed the day before by a member on this side of the House but was negatived by members on the other side of the House-then surely we have a right at least to make some suggestions in an area of provincial jurisdiction.
You are a commie lover.

Mr. Speaker, they can make any remarks they like. I am talking about interference in another jurisdiction. The Tory party is very quick to complain whenever there is any suggestion that the United States might be meddling in Canadian affairs.
I support the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) when he said that we members here represent all Canadians. We are expected as federal members to be Canadians, but that does not stop us from representing our ridings or our province. In all the remarks I have made this afternoon, before supper and again in closing here, what I said I meant for the people in my riding first, for the province of Quebec second, and for the Canadian people third. Because it is all the same. As I said at the opening of my remarks, I have never felt so strongly about an issue. We are not talking just about Bill C-56; we are talking about what Canada is all about.
If we can have no discussions between our provinces today when we still theoretically belong together, then we might as well pack up and go home. Because if we are unfortunate enough to see a Conservative government at some future stage, with the direction in which they are moving we have de facto separation and we will not need a referendum to decide what is going to happen to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that we, of the official opposition, have listened with great interest to the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, the Leader of the New Democratic Party. I want to state immediately, Mr. Speaker, that we fully support the amendment he put forward.
If the Prime Minister was serious in the remarks he made yesterday about the necessity to delay the passage of the bill another month, these remarks can be interpreted to mean that he wants to hold real and serious consultations with the provinces concerning the question we are debating tonight. We, on this side of the House, are convinced the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby will give
May 18, 1978

this government another month during which consultations may be held with the provinces as well as private citizens on the very complex problem that is before us tonight.

I say most regretfully, Mr. Speaker, that in all my years sitting on the left side of the Chair in this House, I have never seen our federal government commit a greater series of errors than they have in the handling of the sales tax case with the provinces which we are discussing tonight. The hallmark of the Prime Minister's and the Ministers of Finance's approach to this matter has been gross incompetence, arrogance and political expediency at the price of hurting national unity.
In spite of the simplistic approach of the hon. member we just heard from, the approach of this government is inflexibly based on the proposition that Ottawa has all the answers and that the provinces are to be consulted but never listened to; that all the conventional wisdom rests here in Ottawa and the provinces can never suggest anything, because once the Prime Minister consults his federal bureaucrats nothing can change no matter how good the suggestions are from the provinces. This shows a complete disregard for the realities of contemporary Canada and its regional and provincial diversities, as well as a complete disregard for the Canadian constitution, provincial powers and provincial jurisdiction.
This matter has been handled by a tired government in complete disarray, a government without direction and without new ideas to challenge Canadians. I have got to add a proviso here. Not so many months ago the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), who has just spoken, said this was the worst government Canadians have had to put up with since the second world war. I would like to go one step further than the hon. member, who reluctantly supports this tired government: the handling of this serious matter has confirmed in the minds of all Canadians once and for all something that we in the opposition have witnessed and have known for many months, namely, that this government now sitting to the right of you, sir, is undoubtedly the worst government we have ever had in Canada since confederation. And I say this regretfully. In speaking to people from coast to coast I find they say this is the worst government, and historians will judge it so. This is the worst government that has sat in office since confederation. It must go and the sooner the better.
Save it for the election.

There might not be an election because this Prime Minister hasn't got the guts. He looks at one poll, and he hasn't got the guts to face the electorate. I cannot say that for the electorate because, frankly, the Canadian people cannot put up with another few months of the worst government since confederation.
When I was a young man I joined the board of a medium sized Canadian company, and at my first session sitting on the board of directors at a directors' meeting I turned to one of my fellow directors and I said, "Is this company strong and healthy?" He said, "My good Heward, it is strong and
Income Tax Act
healthy; it has survived ten successive years of mismanagement!"
When I look at the way this sales tax was handled, I say to the Canadian people do not despair; this is a strong and healthy country because it has survived ten consecutive years of gross mismanagement. But this sort of nonsense has to stop, Mr. Speaker. I spoke to an older constituent of mine who has voted Liberal, who has voted Conservative-he has voted against me as well as for me-and he said, "I am 90 years old and in my 90 years as a Canadian citizen I have never seen a government in Ottawa bungle a single matter as much as the federal government has bungled the sales tax proposition." [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, as for the question under consideration this evening, I categorically ask: Who are the people who support this bill? The Quebec legislature, including each opposition party? No. The people and groups of concerned citizens in Quebec? No. Members of the opposition in Ottawa? No. Mr. Ryan, the great Liberal leader in Quebec? No. And since the federal government reversed its stand earlier this week, the citizens and governments of other provinces? No. The turnabout of the federal government announced this week is the most significant one that I have seen during all the years that I have been in Ottawa. And finally, Mr. Speaker, do several government members sincerely support this bill? No they don't.
Mr. Speaker, there is an amusing saying in English which goes like this: Everybody is out of step but me. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should think about it and for the sake of our country, and the well-being of our Canadian economy, they should withdraw that bill as soon as possible and ask the advice of the provinces in a spirit of understanding and good feeling. They should at least accept the amendment moved by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) this afternoon. And you, hon. members on the government side or rather members from the province of Quebec-I think now of the hon. members for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) and for Compton (Mr. Tessier)-the people of Quebec are looking at you now with much interest. They want to know what is more important: you, the hon. members from the province of Quebec or the legitimate aspirations of the whole Quebec population as expressed by a unanimous vote of the National Assembly and by several private groups in the province of Quebec.
I am calling upon members from the province of Quebec tonight. What is your stand? Because on many occasions, you have talked to me in the halls and said: We are against that! The Minister of Finance is stupid and crazy! It is all nice and easy to say that in the halls of Parliament Hill, in the caucus of the Liberal party, but are you going to stand for the legitimate rights of your fellow-citizens in the province of

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act
Quebec, and speak up on their behalf? You have a great opportunity, right now. Now is your chance, my hon. friends, hon. members from the province of Quebec, to defend the legitimate rights of your fellow-citizens.
I repeat what was said last week at the National Assembly, the population of the province of Quebec is keeping a close eye on you. I would like to know what you the government members of the province of Quebec consider most important, the interests of your own party or the interests of the population of Quebec.
I am pleading with you. Did you listen, as I did, to the opinions expressed by your fellow citizens of the province of Quebec, by the opposition parties in the National Assembly and, since the beginning of this week, by the provincial governments that have spoken against the measure we are debating tonight? I am pleading with each and every member from the province of Quebec regardless of their political party. We should work together to convince the government to withdraw this bill as soon as possible and, in order to remedy the situation, to consult the provinces in a spirit of mutual understanding. It is not too late.
I think and I hope that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) mentioned yesterday afternoon in the House of Commons during the question period that he would probably consult the provinces in a spirit of understanding, that he will be doing so with the full support of the government and some members of the province of Quebec so as to remedy this situation as soon as possible.
On many occasions, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said that we supported the Quebec separatist option because we were in favour of the resolution adopted by the National Assembly concerning the sales tax proposal. Well, let me tell the right hon. Prime Minister that I hate the kind of federalism you and your government have been imposing on Canada for the past ten years. Because of your recent confrontation with the provinces on the sales tax issue, because of you inflexibility, your arrogance, no one has done more than the current Prime Minister of Canada and his government to reinforce the two solitudes and help the separatist cause.
You are not serious!

I could not be more serious. How did the Parti Quebecois come to power? Was it in a spirit of goodwill or nonconfrontation as practised by this government?
What is the situation in the province of Quebec now? I was only too glad to see a federal budget with sales tax proposals that would obviously help the secondary manufacturing sector in the province of Ontario. I am glad about that. In dealing primarily with the secondary manufacturing industry in the province of Ontario, in dealing with the flexible approach to the legitimate demands of Saskatchewan and British

Columbia, I was glad of many things contained in the sales tax proposal.

During the preparation of this budget the federal government showed enough flexibility in terms of the sales tax to accommodate the needs and requirements of the provinces of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Ontario. I ask now: Why not Quebec?

I have before me briefing notes for the consultative task force on tariff negotiations. If the textile industry in Quebec or across Canada got their hands on these there would be a fine how-do-you-do. Let me read just two paragraphs regarding the situation in the province of Quebec vis-a-vis textiles, clothing and furniture. This has nothing to do with separatism or federalism. This report cites that in the Quebec manufacturing sector the overriding issue is one of adjustment to competitive pressures on the traditional sectors of textiles, clothing, footwear and furniture. I hope members opposite will listen to what I say, including my confreres from the province of Quebec. Quebec has borne the brunt of the recent decline in Canada's manufacturing employment. Our data suggest that between October 1976 and October 1977 average manufacturing employment in Canada dropped by 34,000; about 30,000 of this net loss was in Quebec, with the great majority in the traditional sectors. Did hon. members hear that? Are they listening? Thirty thousand jobs lost in Quebec out of 34,000 across Canada in the traditional sectors of shoes, clothing, textiles and furniture. Members opposite wonder why Mr. Parizeau replied with that eminently sensible proposition. And they have the gall to support a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who wants to confront people and call them separatists for supporting this eminently sensible suggestion.
In this package of euphemisms, the last paragraph of the report states:
Some industries will, however, remain the focus for industrial adjustment. These include the traditional sectors of textiles, some clothing, footwear and furni-tu re-
For these industries the policy of the government and its objectives should be to reduce progressively the employment phase. Oh, the government has done that-through increased rationalization behind the necessary minimum of transitional protection.
This government has messed up the economy in the province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker. Let us go from the general to the particular.

In the town of Cowansville, which is in my constituency, the Bruck Mills textile plant employed more than 1,000 workers fifteen months ago. Now, there are only 500 workers left. In one town where there are 12,000 residents we have lost 1,000 jobs in the textile sector. Five years ago, Vilas, a company that
May 18, 1978

specializes in furniture, employed 500 workers. Today the plant is almost closed.
In Cowansville we have two small shoe manufacturing industries which will soon close their doors or go bankrupt as a result of the federal government's policy. The same story goes for the rest of the province of Quebec. The only thing I ask from the members of the opposition is to forget all the stupidities concerning this bill and to support the legitimate requests of the national assembly of our province.

Here is a headline in today's newspaper which states "Yarn mills to close, 200 will lose jobs". Does a headline like this not indicate to the government that we have a particular problem involving textiles, shoes, clothing and footwear?
They don't care.

Hon. members don't care? Are hon. members not listening? For the next five years, three years or four years will you just have a Pavlovian dog responsible for everything coming from the province of Quebec and saying "Separatist, separatist, separatist"? Because if you do, my friends, nobody but you and your Prime Minister will aid the cause of separatism more.
Hear, hear!

I will tell you what happened, Mr. Speaker. [Translation]
Because of the traditional situation, this government thinks it automatically has the Quebec electorate in its pocket. [English]
For this reason, because the Liberals get their electoral support from the province of Quebec automatically, they think Quebec can put up with any insult and any mismanagement of their economy by this government. They think they will still vote Liberal. Wait until the next Gallup poll, Mr. Speaker. The Liberals will see what they have done to the electorate in the province of Quebec on this measure.
This particular budget regretfully was prepared not for the long-term good of Canada and Canadians, but for an election. It was the old Liberal strategy of divide and rule. It was not prepared for serious discussion in this House as we are doing tonight. But once and for all we have caught the Liberal government at their own game. Once and for all both Frenchspeaking and English-speaking Canadians have seen the game of the right hon. Prime Minister-one policy for the rest of Canada and another policy for the province of Quebec.
That is not true.

Once and for all, what was the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) up to? What was the hon. Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) up to, and what was the Prime Minister up to? They were trying to escalate the confrontation between Quebec and the rest of
Income Tax Act
Canada for short-term votes for an election which the Prime Minister did not have the guts to call.
Hear, hear!

The last thing that this Prime Minister and the King government expected to have to do was to come before the House of Commons and justify their chicanery to the people of Canada. Now the chickens have come home to roost and the government is caught, my friends.
Right on.

The government wanted a confrontation during an election. The Liberals wanted to go to Englishspeaking Canada and say: "Only the Liberal party can save you from this big, bad man Levesque and all those terrible separatists". The Liberals were going to confront and confront. Forget Canada, and forget why this Prime Minister makes Mackenzie King look like a statesman.
Hear, hear!

The government took Quebec for granted and thought it could insult Quebec with this proposition. Then it went to the rest of the country and said: "Look how tough we can be with Quebec". Well, my friends, wait until the next Gallup poll is out; it will be seen that it was the biggest backfire in Canadian history.

Ottawa does not have a monopoly on shrewdness when it comes to economic measures. From time to time, provincial governments also have good ideas. I may be repeating myself for the second, the third or even the fourth time, but I submit it is not too late for you to withdraw this bill and to accept as soon as possible, first of all, the amendment proposed by the NDP this afternoon and, second, the proposition made by the National Assembly of Quebec.

What we are being confronted with this evening and during this week proves more than ever-and I agree with the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) on this point-that we are in dire need of constitutional revision. When I think of the wasted ten years since this Prime Minister has taken over, my heart nearly breaks in two. I remember when I greeted my friend, the right hon. Prime Minister, when he came here as a backbencher over ten years ago. I think of the number of times when I sat in the parliamentary cafeteria with him and said to him: "Mr. Trudeau, with our social, cultural and political atmosphere, but moreover because of economic duplication and waste, if there is one thing you can do it is to help bring meaningful constitutional change to Canada as quickly as possible." He said to me: "I have not come up here to do that. The present BNA Act is flexible enough for my needs." Subsequently I found out what he really meant.
I say regretfully, Mr. Speaker, that the Fathers of Confederation drafted the British North America Act feeling that it would always be, in cases of prime ministers, in the hands of

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act
statesmen. But in this case they were wrong. The Prime Minister has used the British North America Act as no other Prime Minister in the history of this country has used it for short-term political advantage and confrontation. Look what we have today. The chickens have come home to roost and we are divided as we have never been divided before. Do hon. members think I say this with any partisan delight? No. I say to members opposite, where are the members from the province of Quebec? Could anything be more obvious than that by supporting the Prime Minister as he sinks with his ship they are flying in the face of every single opinion, not only from the province of Quebec, but from all over Canada?
When I ran a company several years ago and I announced my position, very often my branch managers or section heads revised my opinion. They told me they thought I was wrong. I accepted their advice. Did I think I lost face? Their advice perhaps saved my company. Is it really too much to expect the Prime Minister and this government to forget their pride for a minute and accept a measure that would be good for Canada, particularly for our province? In the name of God I ask him to do this.
It has been cited time and time again-and we have a report in our hands emanating from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-that the traditional sectors of textiles, clothing, footwear and furniture are very strong in Quebec.
[ Translation]
Several members have noted on many occasions that, as far as the traditional sectors are concerned, we import many goods from the other provinces. I agree with you that we do not have the exact figures-and neither have you-but I am under the very strong impression that if we adopt the proposal made by the Quebec National Assembly, this will help enormously not only the traditional sectors within the province of Quebec and low income groups, but also the economy of the other provinces, because of these imports.

What about the fact that we have discussed during this debate, that the measure of returning refunds to the province of Quebec will almost 100 per cent obliterate many of the benefits that the Minister of Finance intended in his original budget speech? When he presented his speech, he said, as reported at page 4319 of Hansard'.
Any further stimulus should obviously be fast-acting. It should encourage consumer spending, not more spending by government. It should offset some of the temporary factors which are pushing up prices. This is particularly important now, on the eve of the start of decontrol.
A reduction on retail sales taxes fits these requirements best, and has the added advantage-
He said this many times in his speech over television and outside.
-of benefitting all those who spend in Canada, even those who do not pay income tax.

About the proposal announced by the Minister of Finance this week, could you, as elected representatives of the province of Quebec, explain to me how this rebate proposal can help the people who pay the sales tax, the poor, who do not pay any income tax? Do not try, because it is impossible to explain the unexplainable!

It is clear that because of the economic mismanagement of this government, the low and middle income people of the province of Quebec are being beaten like nobody else in this country by high inflation and a staggering rate of unemployment. Now the federal government, because of its intransigence, will not budge on this measure. They are proposing a counter-proposal or another proposal that will send rembourse-ments or refunds to people who really do not need them.
I can think of thousands and thousands of people in my constituency and the constituencies of almost every member of the province of Quebec who do not pay income tax but will pay sales tax and will not be helped at all because of this measure. Hon. members opposite know it and I know it.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have created confusion in this confusing debate with all their sophistry. They do not understand and therefore have confused the difference between tax room, tax points and tax mechanism. Will the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister get on their feet in this House and show to us that they really know the difference between tax room, tax points and tax mechanism? They do not. It is for this reason that I and all thinking Canadians realize that with this new proposal this week they have balkanized this country as it has never been balkanized before.

The right hon. Prime Minister has on numerous occasions strongly criticized the province of Quebec when they claimed that separation was already a fait accompli. And now, with such a treatment for the province of Quebec, the federal government and the right hon. Prime Minister in turn claim that with such a policy of reimbursement to Quebec taxpayers federalism is already a fait accompli. We now have the proof, Mr. Speaker. I ask another question to hon. members. Is the sales tax a provincial or federal jurisdiction?

Supposing that at nine o'clock tomorrow evening I invited myself to your house, Mr. Speaker, for dinner. Supposing I not only invited myself for dinner and accepted my own invitation, but I then walked into your house and decided to rearrange all of your furniture and your pictures. Would you not be a little annoyed? Sure you would be. That is what this arrogant, intransigent, confronting government has done with every province, one after the other.

And that is exactly what you are doing with the province of Quebec today.
[Mr. Grafftey.l
May 18, 1978



No wonder this country is divided as it never has been divided before. This government's dividing policies have brought this country almost to its knees. Most thinking Canadians now realize that you do not have to be a good Liberal to be a good Canadian.
The other day I took the Minister of Finance at his word. Yesterday we found out that in March, speaking with the minister of finance from the province of Ontario, on many occasions-

-before the Minister of Finance had introduced his budget here in the House of Commons, the Quebec minister of finance had on many occasions rejected the proposal by the federal Minister of Finance.

Let us be quite clear about it. I am basing my remarks on the fact that I know, and members opposite know, that on at least three occasions before the Minister of Finance presented his budget in the House of Commons, Mr. Parizeau objected to the proposition. Some years ago Mr. Howe said "What's a million?" This Minister of Finance is now saying "What's three million?"
[ Translation]
It is obvious that because of the arrogance of the federal government in applying the rebate formula for the sales tax in the province of Quebec, the Canadian taxpayers will waste at least $3 million.
How many times has the Prime Minister stated both in this House and outside that the federal government should never use tax leverage to force the provincial governments to do something they would not otherwise wish to do? He has said so time and time again.

Why make an exception today? How often did the Prime Minister notice that, because of the taxation powers of the federal government, he should not compel the provinces to take measures they do not want to take. You have the answers. Why make an exception today for the sales tax in the province of Quebec? I wonder why. I am going to tell you why. It is because once again the Prime Minister wants to resort to confrontation and say to the English provinces: I am the only one able to keep Quebec like this! Yes.

Why did the Minister of Finance in announcing this program not tell us how much money was available and then set out the broad lines of his policy, afterwards letting each province administer the details? The government believes all the conventional wisdom exists in Ottawa and that the provinces know nothing. But that is not the main reason they took
Income Tax Act
the action they did. Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance did not want Quebec to agree to this measure. They wanted Quebec not to agree. They made it impossible for Quebec to agree with it because they thought they were going into an election and they wanted a spirit of confrontation so as to escalate the national unity debate and make Canadians forget about the economy.
Hear, hear!

But I say this to members opposite: you have been caught at your own game. There is no election. The gutless Prime Minister backed away from it on the basis of one poll, and now you are in the highest forum in the land trying to explain the inexplicable, trying to explain your chicanery.
You are in bed with the pequistes.

We are in bed with the pequistes! That is the most slanderous remark I have heard for a long time. I am just as good a Canadian as you are. I will fight the pequistes as hard as the hon. member will fight them. But like my father before me, I will fight the Liberal government.

-one policy for the English, another policy for the French, and they wonder how come the country is as divided as it is. [English]
I am not a separatist, I am a federalist. But I detest the kind of intransigent confrontation federalism practised by the worst government since confederation which has divided this country as it has never been divided before. I will fight with my life, like my father before me, in such a cause. We have not forgotten such statements as "Conscription if necessary but not necessarily conscription". The present Prime Minister makes Mackenzie King look like a statesman.
I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue by unanimous consent.
No. We want Paproski!
Does the House give consent for the hon. member to continue?

I do not think hon. members really want me to carry on, but I will say this:

It is not too late. It is not too late. I really hope that the Quebec members and opposition members will remedy the situation. It is not too late. Can you tell me, without saying that I am a separatist, without saying that it is a question of separatism, of federalism. Since the entire population of Quebec and most people outside Quebec consider that the stand taken by the National Assembly is good policy, can you tell me what is wrong with that?

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act

Supporters of the party opposite cannot escalate this sort of thing into a debate on national unity because the whole of the Canadian population has seen that tactic for what it is. So let us get on with the business of governing this country. Let us adopt the amendment proposed by the New Democratic Party. It is not Parizeau's advice, it is the advice of the whole national assembly. I know that members over there would dearly like to resurrect the national unity debate, but they cannot do it now. That is over. So let them get on with the business of this House, withdraw this bill, consult the premiers, admit their errors and do what is good for Canada and for all Canadians, rather than what they think is good for getting votes in the short term.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Demers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize now how very crafty the previous speaker, the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), and the Progressive Conservative party are being. Indeed, in supporting the proposal of the New Democratic Party to delay by a month the study of this bill, the Progressive Conservative party is being very wily, as they know full well what they are about. They have had it confirmed by the statistics. They realize very well that this sales tax cut is of great benefit to the Canadian economy. They have seen it in a decrease in unemployment and inflation. I take my hat off to them. I must say they are crafty because they do not want this government, or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who moved those measures, to get the credit for them.
And when that same party calls for an immediate election, I have serious doubts that it is for the same reason. They do not want the recovery of the Canadian economy, and they want an election right now precisely because they do not want this bill passed. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and the Progressive Conservative party are asking for an election because they have no confidence in their own party; with the Gallup poll indicating a 41 to 41, tie, they want an election because they are convinced they will never reach a higher level than those 41 points. They are convinced of that.
I would like to mention also that the Liberal members in this House, contrary to what the hon. member suggested earlier, fully support the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). The hon. member mentioned statistics earlier and said that in the past year or so 34,000 jobs have been lost in the manufacturing sector in Canada, 30,000 of them in Quebec and said that it was specifically due to our budget. But those jobs were lost in past months and have nothing to do with the budget.
Furthermore, I must confess that when the hon. member recalls that fact he knows full well that it is not true and that those jobs were lost in Quebec over the past year and a half and I can give him a few reasons why those jobs were lost in his riding and more particularly in Cowansville. One of the

reasons is that the minimum wage in Quebec is much too high and the city of Cowanswille is rather close to the U.S. border, the state of Vermont, and Quebec businesses are moving to Vermont where the minimum wage is much lower. Another reason why those jobs were lost mainly in Quebec is that taxes in the province of Quebec are higher and companies are interested in paying fewer taxes and going to invest in another province like Ontario. There is also the threat of the separatist sword and the fact that those very industries moved. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) had better not try to tell me that Sun Life moved out of Quebec because of the Minister of Finance's budget. It is not true. First, they do not pay sales tax. Second, they announced their intention to move long before this budget was introduced.
The hon. member is also misleading the House when he says that the $85 rebate to every Quebecker does not benefit people who do not pay taxes but who must however pay the sales tax. What the government is proposing is quite simply to treat the province of Quebec the same way as the other provinces. In the other provinces if the tax room is $100 and the province occupies that tax room and if poorer people do not benefit from the sales tax cut it is precisely because Mr. Parizeau did not want to give them that credit.
I would also like to ask the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi whether he is serious when he believes that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is the one who is going to stop the separatist movement in the province of Quebec. I am convinced that he is not a separatist. I am convinced that he is a strong federalist. But when he states that Joe Clark is going to stop the rise of separatism in the province of Quebec he makes me laugh. In fact, he makes me laugh so much-
He is the Leader of the Opposition!
Do not say Joe Clark.

Order, please. I suggest to the hon. member that when he refers to a member of this House, he should refer to him by his riding and not by his name.

He makes me laugh so much that a certain number of Quebec separatists are so convinced that they are now working for the Progressive Conservative party. I could name a few whom I know personally in the constituency of Joliette. I could also name some candidates, some people who intend to run for the Progressive Conservative party and whose allegiance is very questionable indeed. Anyway, those are matters with which we will deal during the next election campaign. Mr. Speaker, there are surely many Canadians who have been wondering why the federal government has decided to reduce the sales tax by 3 per cent across the country. The government has reached that conclusion after having sought the advice of several prominent economists, and also after

suggestions made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which had made a study to see how the economy could better perform and had come to the same conclusion as the one that the government accepted.
I would like now to read from the March 1978 publication entitled:
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce: Impact
This is an exact quotation:
If the federal government considers it imperative to stimulate the economy, it is the opinion of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce that this objective would be best achieved by reducing the provincial sales tax by 2 to 3 per cent.
And further on:
That it is quite obvious that the government should maintain the size of its anticipated deficit of $10.5 billion for the fiscal year 1977-78, and warns that cuts in expenditures must be emphasized now and in the future.
We can also read the following:
However, to reduce the high rate of unemployment and the serious underdevelopment of our economy anticipated for this year, the Chamber of Commerce recommends that the federal and provincial governments share on a 50-50 basis the cost of reducing provincial sales taxes.
This same bulletin also contains this paragraph:
If the federal and provincial governments cannot come to an agreement, the Chamber of Commerce suggests as an alternative that the Government of Canada reduce other taxes to obtain the same result; however this alternative will not have any immediate impact on the economy and will take longer to reduce the very visible consumer price index.
I wanted to read this to show you that by reducing sales taxes, the federal government followed the suggestion of economists, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and other organizations specialized in this field.
Also one may wonder why these economists did come to the conclusion that a tax reduction was the most appropriate way to stimulate the economy. First, we all agree that the Canadian economy is a federal responsibility. The federal government is responsible for lessening regional disparities and for stimulating the economy. In general, the provinces do not claim that responsibility.
Statistics show that for the past several months, because they feel insecure, Canadians have been saving money as they have never done before. Reports from banks and caisses populates indicate that there is plenty of money in bank accounts. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, people are saving money instead of consuming goods and thus are not contributing to the health of our economy. As a result, we have to find a way to urge people to spend their money. When sales tax reductions were announced, people were told this: "If you buy within the next six months, you will benefit from a three per cent tax reduction. If you do not buy within these six months, you will forfeit that reduction".
That is direct motivation, actual motivation, because people can readily see on their invoices, on their accounts, that they get a three per cent rebate. By urging Canadians to buy, this legislation will help to put the manufacturing industry back on
Income Tax Act
its feet, and, consequently, companies will hire additional people who, in turn, because they will no longer be unemployed will get larger incomes and will afford to spend more money so as to keep the wheels of the economy turning. We have to get that economic wheel turning again because it has been slow in recent years.
The government also decided to abolish this tax uniformly in all sectors so as not to create any animosity among the provinces and to help equitably and without exception all sectors of the economy. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, it is extremely difficult to abolish the tax in a specific sector, and fraud becomes a high risk, something which the provinces would certainly not have accepted. Right now in Quebec many stoves, fridges, washers and dryers which are taxable appliances are being sold and identified as bedroom sets, living room sets and so forth so that the customer does not have to pay tax. By implementing selective tax cuts, the government of Quebec will lose several million dollars in these tax evasions.
Furthermore, if we had allowed the provinces to act selectively the province of Quebec would have acted as it did, without consulting other provinces. On the other hand the province of Ontario would have said: We wish to cut the sales tax only on products that are made here, such as cars, home appliances and so on. This would have greatly reduced the thrust of that tax act. It should be understood that if the province of Quebec eliminates its 8 per cent sales tax on clothing and furniture it is certainly a very worth-while measure which will encourage Quebeckers to spend more. Those Quebeckers who intended to buy a suit six or seven months from now will probably buy it immediately.
However, 40 per cent of the Quebec production of textiles, knitwear and furniture are sold in other Canadian provinces. It means that the 3 per cent reduction of the sales tax given to all other Canadians will encourage them to buy textiles and furniture made in the province of Quebec. If we had allowed all those provinces to reduce their taxes selectively, they would not have cut them on furniture and textiles that are produced mainly in Quebec.
The fact that this tax is not reduced on all goods in Quebec is a great disadvantage for producers and workers, construction hands, truckers who are many in my riding and who have to pay that 8 per cent tax everytime their trucks need repairs; it would also have helped manufacturing companies producing all kinds of items like chinaware, various types of trailers, tools, household articles, mobile homes, and all sorts of things.
In order to know if a 3 per cent tax cut on all goods instead of an 8 per cent reduction on some items would have been more advantageous for Quebec families, I figured out from statistics available, what proportion of their budget Canadian families with two children spend on furniture and other taxable items. According to statistics, 10 per cent of the family budget is spent on furniture and clothing while 25 per cent of that same budget is spent on taxable items like wallpaper,

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act
paint, cosmetics, home appliances and all sorts of items. So it means that Quebeckers would have benefited much more from a 3 per cent tax cut across the board instead of an 8 per cent cut on a few selected items.
There is also another point that I would like to clear up. I refer to the jurisdiction for provincial sales tax. It has been suggested that the federal government has interfered in a provincial field of jurisdiction. It is quite clear to me that the sales tax is exclusively a provincial matter. In my opinion, it could have been said that the federal government was infringing upon a provincial jurisdiction only if it had imposed its own retail sales tax. But that was not the case. We merely said to the provinces: If you reduce your tax by 3 per cent, the federal government will pay 2 per cent of it. The federal government of course will pay it with taxes collected in other fields which come exclusively under its jurisdiction. Moreover, the provinces did not have to accept that proposal. It was subject to one condition only. We told them: If you withdraw your sales tax, we will pay two percentage points. It was a reasonable offer and they were free to accept it or reject it. Besides, nine provinces out of ten accepted it. However, if they rejected the proposal they certainly could not expect the federal government to refund the money which would have then been owing to them.
However, during the three weeks of negotiations which took place with the Minister of Finance, Mr. Parizeau did not say anything, which seemed to imply that he accepted the proposals as did the federal government and the nine other provinces. But once the nine other provinces had accepted the deal, just after that he lets us know that he wants a special status for the state of Quebec. It is impossible for the Government of Canada to agree to such a proposal because if it did the same offer would have had to be made to the nine other provinces and the negotiations would then have been back to square one. In that line of thought, the economic measures considered would no longer be valid.
The Minister of Finance studied the situation and tried to work out a compromise which the other provinces have accepted. He proposed to Mr. Parizeau to reduce his sales tax not by three percentage points as it had been originally intended, but only by two percentage points on all items. This two percentage point sales tax would be reimbursed completedly by the federal government without any contribution of any kind from the provincial coffers. Yet out of pride Mr. Parizeau refused the offer and by refusing such an offer paid for entirely by the central government as I have mentioned he is penalizing all Quebeckers who could have benefited from this sales tax rebate of two percentage points, all Quebeckers whether they pay income taxes or not. Besides being intransigent, Mr. Parizeau has the audacity to say that he absolutely wants these $186 million to be returned to the treasury of the government of Quebec. The Canadian government cannot accept that and as I said a moment ago the other provinces would not accept

such an injustice and everything would have to be renegotiated. So there was only one solution left and that was to reduce the federal income tax of Quebeckers. As we intend to inject money right now into the Canadian economy, we have therefore decided to give each Quebecker a cheque of up to $85, depending on the income tax he has paid in 1977.
We hope this measure will prompt Quebeckers to consume more goods in order to create jobs. We are also convinced that this measure is one of last resort because there was no choice left since we have not been given that choice and we think that this measure will not bring about the expected benefits the three percentage point reduction of the sales tax on all items would have brought about. However, if by any chance there is still time, I would like the government of the Parti Quebecois to revise its positions before this bill is passed and to decide to reduce its sale tax by the two percentage points which the federal government is willing to pay and thus all Quebeckers, even those who do not pay income tax, would benefit from this measure.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in starting my remarks this evening I want to point out first that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) when speaking yesterday-he should not leave because he is going to receive some good advice if he stays-as recorded in Hansard at page 5524, said:
What I am surprised at is that the opposition, even in the Quebec assembly, make no suggestions as to how to solve this question. They just blame the government. At no point since the beginning of this debate have we received any suggestion on how to resolve this.
That is really laughable and if the minister is listening, as I hope he is, I will tell him how easy it is. I will quote to him a man of whom I had never heard before, an American named Guterman, who said something very wise, and I came across this only today. He said: "Admitting error clear as the score, proves you wiser than before." That is all the Minister of Finance has to do to cure the whole situation. The government has made a bad error and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) seems determined to lock them in the error. I think the Minister of Finance has somewhat more flexibility than the Prime Minister. All he has to do is to admit the error and say that the federal government went about this in the wrong way. He should admit that they did not really try to consult with the provinces; that they did not have it worked out with Quebec when he brought his budget down on April 10; that Quebec has outsmarted them, that Quebec has outfoxed them, that Quebec has been streets ahead of them in sagacity, intelligence, shrewdness, slyness, craftiness-far ahead of this mighty government here in Ottawa. They have been run around the ring, and Mr. Parizeau has had the old ring through the Prime Minister's nose and the Minister of Finance's nose right from the start. Just admit that. Let them admit they made an error and are destroying national unity,
May 18, 1978

and destroying any concept of federalism in Canada if we keep on this course.
Admit that is an error and tomorrow or the next day, or within the next month, if the NDP amendment is carried, let the government withdraw what they have in this bill, pay over to the minister of finance of Quebec, to the government of Quebec or to the province of Quebec what they should pay- that is, the S226 million-participate in the reductions they are making-that is, the complete sales tax reduction on clothing, furniture, footwear, etc.-and that will be it.
It is the simplest kind of thing, Mr. Speaker, but you have to be a bit flexible. The trouble is that the government is not flexible. The Minister of Finance has delivered a ukase, they used to call it in Czarist Russia-a command, an edict, an arbitrary order. They delivered an ultimatum to Quebec which Quebec does not have to accept and which Quebec is not accepting. They made a final proposal or a statement of terms. They have tried to dictate.
I want to tell the Minister of Finance what "consulting" means so we will be on the same wavelength when we consider terms. This is the definition given in the Concise Oxford Dictionary. It stales that "consult" means to seek information or advice from; to take into consideration. Consultation means the act of consulting, deliberation. It does not mean that you call the provincial finance ministers and tell them you are going to take certain action, that you are going to do something and that they then have to agree, or if they express no reservation or no opinion you have consulted them. That is not consultation. That is not asking them for information or advice. That is not taking into consideration their views.
The minister when he called the premier of Newfoundland did not seek information or advice last Friday. He called the premier of Newfoundland when he could not get hold of the minister of finance and told him what he was going to do. He told him he was going to pay this $85 per taxpayer direct to the Quebec taxpayer. I will not say what the premier of Newfoundland told the Minister of Finance on the phone. It is confidential, but I can assure you he did not agree. He did not give him the advice that this was the right thing to do. I will not say what he did tell him. The minister did not consult with the provincial ministers.
The humiliation of the four Atlantic provinces was that before April 10 the Minister of Finance never even met physically with a finance minister from any one of those four provinces. When I asked the minister a question today about whether he had any suggestions from the minister of finance for Newfoundalnd before he brought his budget down on April 10, he said in his reply-and if you look at his reply in Hansard tomorrow you will see what he meant-that he did not have to listen to what the minister of finance for Newfoundland said. He said that they were going to bear 100 per cent of the cost of the tax reduction, so I did not have to listen to him.
Income Tax Act
That is how Newfoundland and the four disadvantaged provinces of Canada are treated by this government here in Ottawa. That is what consultation is. That is what happens to the poor; the poor in resources and the poor in finances. That is the kind of consultation they get from this Liberal government at Ottawa. They are told what is going to happen, and because they are going to be compensated 100 per cent their suggestions are not welcome and not listened to. The minister of finance in Newfoundland did not agree with the six month hoist of this 3 per cent sales tax. He did not want it to come off in October of 1978 just when unemployment is starting to rise again to catastrophic and stratospheric heights in Newfoundland. He did not want that. He wanted it to go on at least until the spring, but he was not listened to because beggars cannot be choosers. That is the federal system we now have operating here in Canada, under Liberal domination for the last ten years. That is co-operative federalism.
Quebec, according to all the statistics, is disadvantaged also, but they are bigger and they have more of a sense of having their own homeland in Quebec. They have a history of every government and every political party in the province fighting for provincial rights in Quebec from 1867 to date. That is what they have, so they are prepared to make the financial sacrifice and make themselves heard and felt.
The minister was very incautious when he tried to consult in his usual way with Quebec, telling Quebec what he was going to do with their tax. Quebec just sat by and let him walk into his own trap, into his own arrogance. He delivered his ukase to Quebec and they told him to kiss their icons. That is what they told him, Mr. Speaker, and rightly so, and I congratulate them. I wish that Newfoundland had told him to kiss their icons also. These are Czarist edicts that come from this great monarchy here in Ottawa. The emperor Trudeau and his cohorts. They had better learn and consult. I have given the definition of consult.
"Dictate" means to prescribe, lay down authoritatively, terms, things to be done; lay down the law, give orders. What the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister tried to do was dictate. This was dictation, not consultation. He could not lay down terms to the province of Quebec. He could not lay down the law to them. He could not prescribe. They were not ready to lie down there, and I congratulate them for it. I do not care if they are pequiste, Union Nationale, Liberal or Conservative in Quebec; they took the right attitude. They were not going to be dictated to by Ottawa. I only wish the other nine provinces had done the same.
On budget night on April 10, the Minister of Finance did not pretend, lucky for him, that the provinces had all agreed. He did not even say there was agreement with nine provinces. What he said, as appears in his speech at page 14, was what he offered to do for them. He said at the bottom of page 14 that the measure can be an outstanding example of fiscal co-ordination, and if all provinces accept the federal offer it will mean such-and-such. There was no pretence that Quebec had accepted this federal dictation, this federal edict, this federal ukase; they did not say they were accepting it. When the

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act
Minister of Finance jumped off the diving board with his proposal on April 10 he had no right to think that Quebec was going to accept it, and the pequiste minister of finance said quite plainly they were not going to accept it. Do not let us hear any more of this nonsense we have heard here about how Quebec fooled them and did not indicate any opposition to this suggestion.
We have a federal system yet the Prime Minister goes on with nonsense about balkanizing the country. If Quebec is allowed to lower its own direct sales tax the way it likes, it is going to balkanize the country. It is going to stop the free flow of goods. Don't they realize we have a federal system and that the very fact that provinces have sales taxes means they can interfere with the flow of goods? In Newfoundland we have no retail sales tax on food, clothing or footwear. In other provinces they are taxing the people with a retail sales tax. We have an 11 per cent tax but in Newfoundland we do not tax clothing, footwear and food. Other provinces do. Other provinces have their own purchasing policies.
In Quebec they will only enter into contracts with firms headquartered in Quebec. We have all kinds of situations that interfere with the free flow of goods-whatever phraseology you want to use. Quebec is not balkanizing the country if Quebec has a sales tax and decides to exempt certain things and not exempt certain other things. It is exercising the same prerogative as Newfoundland, P.E.I., New Brunswick and others, and they have done it every year, as the federal government has done in respect of tariffs and federal sales tax. There is no balkanization involved.
If Quebec is permitted to go ahead and do what it is doing and still receive federal financial assistance, no other province can complain because it did not get the same deal. They did not stick out for the same deal. They gave in, they surrendered, they collapsed. They did not have the backbone to stand up on their hind feet because most of them were not in the financial position to do so. They did not do that, but Quebec did. Some of them tried but they did not hold out to the bitter end. Quebec did because it is more important to them to preserve their own rights in their own province than other considerations. There was no agreement so the government cannot complain that Quebec has not gone along with them. They knew there was no acceptance by them at all.
Now, if we look at May 17 Hansard again, the Prime Minister is again mixed up. Some may say it is only semantics. At page 5507 the Prime Minister said:
-The Minister of Finance reached an agreement with nine of the provinces and the provinces agreed to this after three weeks of talks.
They did not agree, Mr. Speaker. There was not an agreement with nine of the provinces. There wasn't any such agreement. Nine provinces have acquiesced, not agreed. There was no agreement from the province of Newfoundland. The province of Newfoundland never consented to this. An agreement is where two parties agree freely and voluntarily to enter into an arrangement with one another. Newfoundland, for

example, never did that. They accepted the gratuity handed to them by the Government of Canada when they made some suggestions as to how it should be done; otherwise they were ignored.
I do not believe there was a genuine agreement with any of the provinces except Ontario. It was Darcy McKeough's brainwave in the first place and naturally Ontario agreed, but not the other provinces. The Prime Minister is mixed up. He said:
So I would be very surprised if because the province of Quebec, having failed to state its position before the budget, is now coming out with a scheme which tends to balkanize the Canadian market, the other provinces would want to go in the direction of that balkanization.
Well, I do not care whether they do or do not. I see nothing wrong if the province of Ontario had reduced all tax on automobiles, if that was their choice and another province reduced all tax on something entirely different. As long as the consumer was getting the break and the economy was being stimulated, what difference does it make? The only difference is that this is an arrogant, inflexible government that wants to make the provinces bow to their will.
The greatest sin, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister has committed in this connection was on April 14. You would expect the Prime Minister of this country not to be a cheap politician, or at least not to show that he is a cheap politician as easily as some other people might be. When I questioned him on April 14, Mr. Speaker, in the House of Commons in the question period, asking him why Quebec was not permitted to do what they wished to do, the Prime Minister said at page 4507 of Hansard:
I find the opposition supporting a separatist government in Quebec-
And on the same page, Mr. Speaker:
I was dealing with the support given by the Tory party to the scheme put forward by the separatist party of Quebec.
That is an attempt to paint anyone who disagreed with the Prime Minister and his policies as separatists, Mr. Speaker. But now he is painted into a corner because Claude Ryan and the Liberal members of the legislative assembly in Quebec, the Union Nationale members, the Social Credit members and all members of the Quebec national assembly are now, by that definition, painted as separatists.
Agreement does not mean, Mr. Speaker, accepting or acquiescing in ultimatums. That is why there were no agreements. On May 16 the Minister of Finance at page 5451 of Hansard said:
I am surprised that a national party wants to save the neck of the Parti Quebecois.
That was the Minister of Finance's response to questions by our spokesman on federal-provincial relations, the hon. lady for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), "that a national party wants to save the neck of the Parti Quebecois." It is the federal government that is saving their neck. It is the federal government that has by its stupidity, by its arrogance, by its inflexibility, given this neck tremendous additional strength.
May 18, 1978

What we want to do is to save Canada, Mr. Speaker. To save Canada it is necessary to remove the Prime Minister and his government from office in this country, not save the neck of the Parti Quebecois. They can look after their own necks. As somebody once said, "some neck, some chicken". Winston Churchill said that. I tell you the Parti Quebecois has got a neck that the Prime Minister of this country cannot deal with. The people that are going to be able to deal with that neck are we on this side when we take office.
Hear, hear!

The Prime Minister's position, Mr. Speaker, was given also yesterday in Hansard, May 17. Speaking at page 5508 he said:
The minister has taken a position, and this position is supported by the government and by every member on this side of the House.
He was intimating that there was a surge of support over there. There is one "Serge" I heard is not supporting them. And further down he said:
We have taken a position and we are going to stick with it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister sticks with it then certainly he is finished as an apostle of national unity in this country. What the Prime Minister is practising is rigor mortis federalism. The Liberal party and the government are dying and they are entering into a state of rigor mortis. The old co-operative federalism is gone and it is rigor mortis federalism now. They never deviate. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance decide what federal-provincial relations are going to mean. They decide what the provinces will do with their sales tax; they decide what Quebec is going to do; they decide what Newfoundland is going to do; and they are able to enforce their decision because Newfoundland got complete reimbursement from the federal treasury. Quebec did not.
When somebody comes up with a better suggestion, "No, we won't budge, we won't move, we are stiff, we are rigid, we are Trudoids, we're Liberals in power in Ottawa, we have rigor mortis, we can't move a muscle, we can't respond." So co-operative federalism has now degenerated into rigor mortis federalism.
And to the death of the Liberal party.

And to the death of the Liberal party, that is good. We think that that is an advantage. And from the decaying corpse of the Liberal party will spring in a few years' time perhaps some fresh flowers such as those that adorn the Prime Minister new when he speaks to us in the House in question period.
Here we are, Mr. Speaker. We can have a unitary state. If we want a unitary state-and I presume the people of Canada deserve that-we could vote to do that, do away with federalism and we won't have any problems. We could have the government in Ottawa decide everything, as they do in the United Kingdom. But since the people have not decided that yet, Mr. Speaker, we have in Canada vast inequities because we have provinces. We have in the province of Newfoundland
Income Tax Act
a gasoline tax of 25 cents a gallon; we have in Alberta no gasoline tax and in the other provinces a very small gasoline tax. Well, we are prepared to put up with our high gasoline tax if it means that we have our own local government, at least for the province of Newfoundland. If everything is not decided up here in Ottawa, we are prepared to sacrifice something. We know that if we lived in Alberta we would pay no gasoline tax at all.
The country in that sense is balkanized. We know that we are paying 11 per cent sales tax and in Alberta they are paying no sales tax. It appears to be unfair. Presumably, if we wiped out all ten provinces we would all be treated exactly the same from one end of the country to the other. But would we want that? We would no longer be a federal state. That is where this government is leading us to. If Quebec wants to make its own decision on what exemptions it is going to grant in its own direct sales tax, Mr. Speaker, and that is not permitted because it is supposed to be balkanization, then that means the end of federalism. That is where we are headed to if the Prime Minister's attitude is the one that wins the day.
Look at the statement put out by the Minister of Finance on May 15. Just look at this for arrogance, Mr. Speaker. Page 1:
I have also written to Mr. Parizeau today to explain my resolution of the dispute over the retail sales tax reduction in the province of Quebec.
How can the Minister of Finance of Canada by himself solve this dispute? He is a nice man and I genuinely like him, but he has been too long in office. Just listen again to the monumental arrogance of that statement:
I have also written to Mr. Parizeau today to explain my resolution of the dispute over the retail sales tax reduction in the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Finance of Canada has spoken. He is saying: "The dispute has been resolved. This is my ukase, I am like a Russian czar, when I speak everyone must bow". This is a statement issued by the Government of Canada. Now, Mr. Speaker, we proceed with the statement at page 2:
The federal government should not be party to an arrangement which interferes with the flow of goods in the Canadian common market.
What bourgeois! It pays Newfoundland hundreds of millions of dollars in tax equalization, and Newfoundland uses it to interfere with the free flow of goods because Newfoundland will use it to buy Newfoundland first if it can, the same as Quebec does, the same as Ontario does. The government is in a conspiracy to interfere with the flow of goods in the Canadian common market every day of the week with the money they are giving the other provinces through tax equalization and the like. So don't give us such statements as: "The government will not be a party to such an arrangement." The government in its arrogance does not even know what arrangements it is party to any more.
On page 3 the minister has this to say:
I have discussed this arrangement with my colleagues in each province. They all told me they would have preferred Quebec acceptance of the original proposal.
I do not believe it. I do not believe the statement "They all told me they would have preferred Quebec acceptance of the

May 18, 1978
Income Tax Act
original proposal." I do not believe that for a minute. They did not all tell them that. Ele said "I have discussed this arrangement". This was a telephone call to the premier of Newfoundland: "Premier, this is what I am doing. I am going to solve this thing by paying $85 per capita back to the taxpayers in Quebec." That was the discussion. There was no discussion in any sense of "discussion" as we free people know a discussion to be-I give my views and you give yours. So that is another incorrect statement.
In his letter to the minister of finance of Quebec on April 21 there are the same kind of errors polluting the whole letter as attached to that statement. The minister laid down certain conditions. On page 2 he writes:
Third, it was necessary that the proposed measure apply uniformly in all provinces.
Why? It is only necessary because the Minister of Finance says it is necessary. There is no immutable law of the universe that says it was necessary and had to apply uniformly in every province. And it did not. In British Columbia and Saskatchewan they had a different arrangement. Who is the Minister of Finance trying to fool?
On page 3 of that same letter this appears:
However, the federal government could not envisage bilateral agreements aimed at exempting one product in one province and another in another province.
Why not? The whole sales tax arrangement provincially has that flavour, so why not? I have already made the point about tax equalization and the rest of it.
The whole thing is riddled with inconsistencies. This is a government that can no longer see. It has had so much power for so long, it has had financial power vis-a-vis the provinces for so long, that it now automatically has got itself convinced that these silly mistaken statements are correct. It is an awful shame and tragedy, Mr. Speaker.
The exception in Quebec on clothing, footwear, furniture and textiles is not just for Quebec manufactured products. That also applies to imported products. That applies to products that come in from other provinces. They have not made an exemption just for Quebec manufactured goods. To exempt clothing, surely, is a proper thing. The lower income people spend most of their income on food, clothing and shelter, so furniture and clothing are the kinds of things you would like to see a major reduction of sales tax on. There is nothing wrong with that. It is just that the federal government had not dreamed it up first. They thought they were going to apply the iron fist to a government that decided to do something they had not thought of.
This becomes the great sales tax swan dive. It is just as well for the Minister of Finance to realize that the swan has become the ugly duckling. The darling swan of the Quebec caucus is now the ugly duckling of the Quebec caucus, with his strident quack-quacks in this chamber and his quack-quacks outside of the chamber; and the Prime Minister's quack-quacks are just quack-quacks. They are ugly ducklings now. The old white feathers are gone off the old swan. The graceful swan that came into this chamber a few months ago as the new

Minister of Finance has turned into an ugly quack-quack. His statements make no more sense than a quack-quack, Mr. Speaker. I wish I knew what the French is for "quack-quack". This is the old sales tax swan dive. The sooner the minister takes that swan dive, the better.

What did the finance minister in Newfoundland say about this proposal to rebate taxes to the individual taxpayer in Quebec when he heard about it? I quote the minister of finance of Newfoundland. He said:
.. . certainly not an action that could be construed in any way as a unifying measure.
Even the province of Newfoundland, which has to accept federal largesse because we poor devils down there have an 11 per cent sales tax and cannot turn down the opportunity to have it go away even for six months, even we have the right to express an opinion. Our government's opinion is that it is "not an action that could be construed in any way as a unifying measure". No, it is a measure that is disunifying this nation. It is unifying the nation against the government. That may be the only good part about it. They are going to transfer and make a payment to Newfoundland and other provinces which they could not refuse.
What consultation was there with the government of Newfoundland before April 10? A telephone conversation with our minister of finance. Imagine, an important matter of federal-provincial relationships like this and the four Atlantic provinces' ministers got telephone calls to tell them what was happening!
The Minister of Finance went out west and met with the western ministers. He met with the Quebec and Ontario ministers but he didn't even bother to meet with the four maritime provinces. That is how important this was looked upon, this major excursion into the change in our whole federal-provincial relations.
When the government says, "We are not going to allow the provinces to act selectively," the government is saying, "We, the government, are not going to allow you in your own constitutional jurisdiction, with your own poor little old retail sales tax-we are not going to allow you to do what you like with it. Not with our money. We want you to reduce the tax and give stimulus to the economy, but when you want to reduce it one way that we do not agree with, we are going to tell you no, you can't do it with our money." That's the government's position.
Should the federal government not have said to Newfoundland, "Gentlemen, put back your sales tax on clothing so you will be uniform with Quebec. We are not going to allow Quebec to eliminate it. Newfoundland has got to put it back on clothing and P.E.I. has to put it back; and Newfoundland, you have got to put it back on footwear so that you will be uniform with the other provinces. P.E.I., you have to put it back on footwear. You can't exempt these any longer because if you exempt them when you are getting some help from us to
May 18, 1978

reduce it 2 or 3 per cent over all you are going to balkanize the country."
That is just as intelligent as telling us now that Quebec is not to be allowed to make selective cuts, that it is going to balkanize the country. They have the balkans on their mind over there. They are going to balkanize the electorate of this country. They have already done that.
We have come now to a position where everyone in Canada who takes any interest in these matters can see how real an attitude this government takes toward national unity. When it has an opportunity to do something constructive in a national unity sense with the province of Quebec, it tries to act like a Russian emperor and crush any opposition in that province. Then, when every other party in the province backs the Parti Quebecois government, the Prime Minister gets more rigid than ever, more inflexible than ever. Rigor mortis has set in. He is determined that he is not going to budge.
Mr. Speaker, I have given my advice to the Minister of Finance. I repeat it in ending my remarks-admitting error clears the score and proves you wiser than before. If it helps, Mr. Speaker, I will admit that I have been wrong at times, too.
Hear, hear!
